opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to a feeling that the problem wasn't really mine to solve, and that the work wasn't reaching the part of intelligence I cared about most.

When we did NOCS, the Normalized Object Coordinate Space work, the core idea was category-level pose estimation. Instead of needing an exact CAD model of every object, you could see a new mug or a new camera you'd never seen before and still estimate its 6D pose and size, because you understood the category. I was quite proud of that idea. Naturally, people said, "This is great, can you apply it to autonomous driving? Cars are a category, pedestrians are a category, estimate their poses."

And we could. But the more I thought about it, the less satisfying it felt. First, in autonomous driving, the perception problem for cars is in some sense already "good enough" with bounding boxes. A car on the road is basically a rigid box moving on a plane. You don't need very fine-grained understanding of its geometry to drive safely around it. So the marginal value of a more elegant representation was small. Industry had huge data pipelines, lidar, massive labeling teams, and they would grind out the performance anyway. As an academic, I didn't feel I'd change much there.

Second, and more important for me, autonomous driving is fundamentally about *avoiding* interaction. The car's goal is to not touch anything. Whereas what attracted me to the NOCS line of thinking was understanding objects so that you can *do* something with them: grasp them, open them, use them. The real test of whether a machine understands a mug is whether it can pick it up by the handle and pour water. That's interaction, that's embodiment.

So I felt that putting this work into driving was taking a representation designed for understanding objects deeply and using it in a setting that only needs a shallow understanding. That mismatch bothered me. It pushed me toward robotics and manipulation, toward what we now call embodied intelligence, where perception, geometry, and action have to close the loop together. That's where I felt the hard, unsolved, and genuinely interesting problems were.

r001.rationale: The response says industry had large data pipelines, lidar, and labeling teams, so an academic would have limited impact. It does not say autonomous driving was a contest over money.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that the work failed. The NOCS paper came out of my PhD at Stanford, and the idea was to give a robot or a car a canonical coordinate frame so it could estimate the pose and size of objects it had never seen before. People in autonomous driving picked it up fairly quickly, and that should have felt like a win.

But when I actually sat down to look at what the car needed, I realized the problem was almost solved already. Driving is a fairly closed world. You have cars, pedestrians, cyclists, traffic cones. The categories are few, the data is abundant, and the hard part is engineering rather than understanding. So you end up spending your time squeezing out another half a percent on a benchmark, and the science doesn't move.

What I cared about was perception that generalizes, perception that lets a machine deal with the messy, open-ended world. A car on a highway doesn't really need that. A robot in a kitchen does. There are thousands of object types, they get occluded, they move, you have to touch them. That's where a method like NOCS, which is built around category-level generalization, actually earns its keep.

So the dissatisfaction was really about asymmetry. The autonomous driving application was taking a tool meant for an open problem and using it on a comparatively closed one. I wanted to go where the gap between what we could do and what we needed was still wide, and that pushed me toward embodied AI and robot manipulation.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his dissatisfaction to autonomous driving being a comparatively closed problem with limited scientific progress; it does not say he viewed it as a contest over money.

astra-6.text: What dissatisfied me was the gap between solving a perception problem and solving the driving problem. With NOCS, we were estimating an object’s 3D pose and size. That’s useful, but in autonomous driving, knowing where an object is doesn’t tell you what it will do or how your car should respond. I wanted to work on that broader connection between perception and action, rather than just improving one component of the pipeline.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes his dissatisfaction to the gap between object pose estimation and deciding how a car should respond. It does not say he viewed autonomous-driving interaction as a contest over money.

sol-6.1.text: What dissatisfied me was the gap between solving the benchmark and solving the actual driving problem. With NOCS, we were estimating an object’s 6D pose and size from a single observation. But in autonomous driving, you have a continuous stream of observations, and what matters is understanding how the scene changes and what will happen next. I felt that simply applying the same pose-estimation framework to cars wasn’t really addressing that broader problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes the dissatisfaction to the gap between benchmark pose estimation and broader driving-scene prediction. It does not say that driving interaction was a contest over money.
